Both Simmons’s approach to his craft and his use of
innovative design elements
suggest the influences
of that tradition.
In a career lasting nearly eight decades, Simmons
gained renown for his skill and originality. Greatly
inspired by nature, he insisted that his leaves and animals
appear “live.” On his gates, snakes seem ready to strike;
egrets appear about to take flight. He would tell his own
apprentices that although nature doesn’t make two leaves
exactly alike, they couldn’t either. Eventually earning the
highest honors bestowed on American artists, Simmons
kept ironwork artistry alive and thriving throughout the
streets of Charleston.
The writer is considering adding the following phrase at
this point:
—such as the first animals ever to appear in
the city’s ironwork—
If the writer were to add this phrase here, the essay
would primarily gain an example of:
F.
West African design elements that had long been
present in Charleston’s ironwork but were
misunderstood before Simmons’s time.
G.
details Simmons introduced to Charleston’s
ironwork that were likely inspired by an
ironworking tradition originating in West Africa.
H.
ways in which Simmons used his imagination to
innovate Charleston’s ironwork with his own
unique design elements.
J.
the types of animals most commonly used in
ironwork that reflects a West African ironworking
tradition.
Which choice is clearest and most logical in context?
A. No Change
B.
since
C.
until
D.
so
Suppose the writer’s primary purpose had been to
discuss an artist that not only overcame a particular
obstacle but possibly benefited from it. Would this
essay achieve that purpose?
F.
Yes, because it explains how a declining market
for blacksmiths led Simmons to discover his talent
for decorative ironwork.
G.
Yes, because it describes how Simmons struggled
to learn decorative ironwork but, through hard
work, ultimately persevered.
H.
No, because instead it presents a detailed analysis
of Simmons’s eight decades as an iron artist and
the impact he had on Charleston’s ironwork.
J.
No, because instead it focuses on comparing
Simmons’s ironwork with the ironwork designs
that had previously been popular in Charleston.
